svg.text: ME/CFS symptom mapping – question tree and granules
Granule WHAT is felt or done – one sensation or ability (e.g. PN1 pain).
Facet UNDER WHICH CIRCUMSTANCE – where, when, how much, which activity (e.g. region = head). Only some facets are asked in the tree; they appear as “facet · …” under the answer.

svg.text: Rating of one's health as a whole.
How much the illness restricts life as a whole, from bedbound to normal.
How tired vs. energetic one feels overall; fatigue and available energy are
the two poles of one axis.
Tiring unusually fast DURING physical effort.
Tiring unusually fast DURING mental effort.
Worsening of symptoms AFTER exertion, often delayed, slow recovery.
COG · Brain fog / thinking (26 of 58 studies)
Keeping attention on one thing over a period of time.
Attending to more than one thing at once (e.g. several speakers, task +
How fast thinking runs; slowed thought.
Taking in and understanding information, read or heard.
Retaining and recalling information; everyday forgetting.
Retrieving the right word when speaking or writing.
Putting thoughts into spoken or written language.
Losing orientation or the thread: not knowing where/when, feeling muddled.
Waking up during the night and staying awake.
Waking much earlier than intended and not falling asleep again.
Not feeling rested after sleep, regardless of duration.
Feeling drowsy or needing to sleep or nap during the day.
Sleeping mainly by day and being awake at night.
PAI · Pain (incl. head, chest) (22 of 58 studies)
How much pain gets in the way of daily activities (impact, not intensity).
Feeling of restricted, stiff movement (e.g. joints), distinct from pain.
Pain from stimuli that normally hurt little or not at all, incl. pain
CAR · Heart, circulation, breathing (19 of 58 studies)
Not being able to stay upright; symptoms build up when sitting/standing and
Feeling dizzy or faint, vision greying, nearly or actually passing out.
Heart racing, pounding or beating irregularly.
Trouble getting enough air or catching one's breath.
How much energy was spent or how much was done.
How much activity one can do before it costs something: fewer other activities
the same day, or reduced capacity in the following days. Measured as the cost
of a given activity (FUNCAP). Cause of fatigability (EN2/EN3) and crashes
Being able to sit or stand upright for a while without symptoms forcing you to
Activities that need force or raise the heart rate (lifting, carrying,
How much health reduces work and daily activities compared with normal /
Deliberately keeping activity below one's limit to avoid crashes (behaviour,
How much emotional problems reduce work and daily activities.
How much health (physical or emotional) limits social activities.
Feeling nervous, tense or worried; opposite pole: calm and peaceful.
Feeling down, low or blue; opposite pole: happy.
Feeling under pressure or unable to cope with demands.
BOD · Other body symptoms (8 of 58 studies)
Light that others find normal is unpleasant, straining or makes symptoms
Sounds that others find normal are unpleasant, straining or make symptoms
Vibration (e.g. car, train, machines) is unpleasant or makes symptoms worse.
Eyes cannot focus; the image is blurred or narrowed.
Smell or taste weaker, lost or distorted (e.g. after COVID).
Diarrhoea, constipation or cramping of the bowel.
Feeling of a swollen, full belly.
Problems passing urine: urgency, frequency, waking at night to urinate.
Muscles produce less force than normal, even before tiring.
Small involuntary muscle contractions or jerks.
Precision of movements: clumsy, dropping things, missing targets.
Keeping stable on one's feet; feeling one might fall.
Feeling cold, shivering or having cold hands/feet without a cold environment.
Feeling as if one has a raised temperature (not a measured fever).
Switching between hot and cold for no reason, over the day.
Coping badly with heat or cold in the environment.
Sweating more than the situation explains.
Weight going down or up without trying.
Feeling unusually unwell from small amounts of alcohol.
Pain or scratchiness in the throat.
Swollen or tender glands, e.g. neck, armpits.
Feeling ill as with flu: aching, feverish, run-down.
Raised body temperature (ideally measured; NE2 = only feeling feverish).
How often one gets infections and how long recovery takes.
Feeling sick from smells, chemicals, foods, medication or mold.
Not in the check-in tree (periodic only)
Better or worse than at a reference point (protocol start, a year ago).
